context: A fisherman has helped the shipwrecked Apollonius and directed him toward the city. This preceding context is English support, not an added Old English reading assignment.
paragraphs: After these words he went along the road that had been shown to him, until he came to the gate of the city and went in there. While he was considering whom he might ask for support to live on, he saw a naked boy running along the street. The boy was anointed with oil and girded with a sheet, and carried in his hand the equipment for young men's games belonging to the bath. He called out in a loud voice and said, ‘Listen, citizens! Listen, strangers, free and enslaved, noble and low-born! The bath is open.’

When Apollonius heard that, he stripped off the half cloak that he had on and went into the bath. As he looked at each one of them at their activity, he sought his equal, but he could not find him there in the company. Then Arcestrates, king of that whole country, suddenly arrived with a great company of his men and entered the bath. The king began to play ball with his companions. Apollonius joined the king's game, as God willed, and, running, caught the ball and sent it back to the playing king, struck with swift speed. Again he sent it back; he struck quickly, so that he never let it fall. The king then recognized the young man's skill, so that he knew that he had no equal in the game. Then he said to his companions, ‘Go away from here; this young man, as it seems to me, is my equal.’

When Apollonius heard that the king praised him, he ran quickly and approached the king. With a skilled hand he swung the top or ball so swiftly that the king felt as if he had been changed from old age to youth. After that, on his royal seat, Apollonius served him agreeably; and when the king went out of the bath, Apollonius led him by the hand, and then himself turned away from there along the road by which he had come before.

After Apollonius had gone away, the king said to his men, ‘I swear by our common welfare that I never bathed better than I did today, through the service of I know not what young man.’ Then he turned toward one of his men and said, ‘Go, and find out what that young man is who served me so well today.’

The man then went after Apollonius. When he saw that Apollonius was wrapped in a dirty cloak, he returned to the king and said, ‘The young man whom you asked about is a shipwrecked man.’ Then the king said, ‘By what do you know that?’ The man answered him and said, ‘Even if he himself keeps it silent, his clothing reveals him.’ Then the king said, ‘Go quickly, and tell him that “the king asks you to come to his meal.”’

interpretive_limits.point: The literal game/play carried in the hand is rendered contextually as equipment for games. Preserve the exact plegan source token and the original Latin gloss separately; the translation does not certify an unrestricted new lexical sense.

Geslægene agrees with the accusative ball; Cook calls the participle awkward. The translation preserves the passive participial relation instead of silently changing the source to a finite he struck. A smoother English rendering may redistribute the participial phrase while retaining its agent/patient meaning.

The natural action sequence makes the king the first sender-back and Apollonius the next striker; hine denotes the ball. The supplied reading should mark contextual actor inference separately from masculine-singular morphology.

This intentionally literal he/he/his rendering leaves the unclear source antecedents open. Cook's note6 does not license replacing the Old English clause with its Latin parallel or grading a single antecedent as certain.

The actual Old English has swang ðone top. Cook compares a Latin account of rubbing him with ointment and tentatively identifies top with the ball. The model retains the printed action and object and records the discrepancy instead of silently replacing them with the Latin action. The earlier shoulder shorthand was erroneous: the quoted Latin contains no shoulder noun.

The explicit noun replacements in the English translation are interpretive clarification: Apollonius serves and leads the king, then leaves. Notes14–16 support the latter assignments; the actual Old English pronouns must remain unchanged.

The source lacks the expected closing quotation mark after the king's oath. The English translation closes that speech before the next narrator clause; this is declared punctuation clarification. Nā(t) ic is interpreted within the phrase concerning the unknown young man's service.
Hwæt asks for the young man's identity or status, as originalnote7 prompts; idiomatic who is possible if the grammatical distinction is explained.

The translation deliberately preserves the source's combination of tell him that and the message's second-person address. A smooth ordinary indirect paraphrase can explain the meaning but must not replace the exact source for analysis.
